vignette:
She was thirty-four the first time she tried to tell someone. It came out in pieces, like a vase she’d dropped and then tried to glue back together—only she couldn’t find all the shards. The man was a collector, someone a gallery owner had introduced her to. He praised her work, said he wanted to commission a large piece for his home. She met him in his studio—a converted warehouse with high ceilings and northern light. He poured wine. She remembers the taste of metal, the weight of his hand on her shoulder. And then the rest of it, the part she still cannot shape into words, not even now, twenty-nine years later.

For a long time she did not call it rape. She called it “that night,” or “the thing with the collector.” She told herself she had been naive. She stopped taking commissions from strangers. She locked the door to her studio, even during the day. But she kept working. Clay and stone and sometimes bronze, rough textures, hands that seemed to grip nothing. Her figures became smaller, more closed. She would spend hours carving the same curve of a shoulder, then smash it with a hammer and start over.

Now she is sixty-three. Her hands are still strong, but they shake when she reaches for a tool. She works in a small studio behind the house she shares with her husband, a retired librarian who reads aloud to her in the evenings. She listens, but the words sometimes dissolve into static, and she finds herself staring at the door, checking the lock for the third time. He does not know about the collector. She has never told him. The secret sits inside her like a stone she has swallowed, heavy and cold.

She avoids the news. She avoids movies with violence. She avoids the medical office where a male doctor once touched her shoulder during an exam and she froze, unable to breathe, her whole body going numb. She avoids the scent of red wine. She avoids certain streets, certain hours of the day. Her world has become smaller, a series of safe places: the studio, the bedroom, the narrow path between them.

Sleep comes hard. She wakes at three in the morning, her heart slamming against her ribs, certain she heard footsteps. Her husband sleeps beside her, untroubled. She does not wake him. Instead she lies still, cataloguing the sounds of the house, the creak of the pipes, the wind against the window, the shape of the shadows. She has memorized every inch of that ceiling. She has imagined different versions of the night with the collector: what she could have said, where she could have run. None of them change anything.

Her work has changed too. She no longer sculpts human forms. She makes abstract shapes—broken rings, sharp angles, vessels with holes that do not hold water. Recently she started a piece that she cannot finish. It is a sphere, smooth and closed. Every time she picks up her chisel, her hands cramp. She leaves it on the worktable, covered in a cloth. She does not know why she cannot touch it.

She is tired all the time. She forgets appointments. She has stopped returning calls from old friends. When her husband suggests a trip, she feels her stomach tighten. She says maybe later. She is not sure what she is afraid of. She only knows that the memory lives behind her eyes, vivid and waiting, and that she spends most of her energy trying not to look at it directly. Some days she thinks the collector is still in her life, even though he died five years ago. She read his obituary online and felt nothing—then felt everything, a nausea that lasted for hours.

She does not believe she is sick. She believes she is fine. She believes the past is past. She believes the only thing that matters is the next piece of stone, the next line she can carve, the next morning she can walk into her studio and close the door. She does not know why she cannot stop checking the lock.
